A REEVE WHO DOES NOT KNOW WHO PAID, A MAN WHO WILL NOT SELL WHAT HE KNOWS, AND COAL AT TWICE THE FIGURE.** A reeve of about fifty-nine on a harbor on that coast road has had his coal and his water paid twice in a fortnight by a name that is the name of an office, and asks for it to be written in a minute, and the minute is read back to him. **A man of about thirty-eight in that harbor will not sell what he knows and gives a reason that names three men out of a coat and nine days and the fact that he was the second man, and was not asked a second time by anybody and was not shown the sheet.** The holder of that writ is not in that harbor and his wage still comes in, and the reason is in the second column.
7. **CHAPTER 457, TUESDAY THE NINETEENTH. THE FIFTY-SECOND WAGE TUESDAY, A CHAMBER WITH A STOVE IN IT, AND A FOUR-INCH MARK.** The wage column does not move and fifty-two weeks stand fallen due. A bell-shaped chamber with a deck plate, a stove, a stove pipe and a gauge goes down onto an exposed shelf in about nine fathoms and stands on it, and the gauge reads eighty-four pounds on a face of a hundred and fifty, and that reading is not a depth reading. **About ninety yards off the port bow there is a cut about four inches long, square at both ends, with thin silt on it, put in as about three weeks old by the man who was in that bell.** Nine men said nothing about it and one of them asked whether anybody was going to say it out loud in front of the master, and the answer was no.
8. **CHAPTER 458, WEDNESDAY THE TWENTIETH. A GASKET, A TENDER'S CHAIN WEIGHT, AND A MAN WITH NINE FEET OF SOUND MISSING.** Everything about the descent is on a slate before anybody goes down: a tender of about thirty-eight on the surface and not in the boat, an air limit of forty minutes as a figure, an independent line, a cutoff the tender can pull without asking, and a reason with the hour. A gasket lets go at about ten to three and the chain weight comes over the rail without a word to anybody. **A man of about twenty-nine comes up in about six minutes and cannot hear out of the left side of his head, and is not thanked, not made a casualty, not sent home, and goes on working, and no figure is set against it because a man on a mole cannot check what a man can hear.** He says he heard a noise before anything that makes a noise; the man who went down first says he heard nothing and will not say the other man is wrong. Both accounts are entered. **There are now eight accounts in that leaf that do not agree with each other and none of the eight has been settled.**
9. **CHAPTER 459, THURSDAY THE TWENTY-FIRST. THE MOUTH OF THE TRENCH, A PAPER THAT ANSWERED, AND A CUT IN SOMEBODY ELSE'S LEAD.** The trench is found in about twenty-two fathoms and the water at its mouth comes up about two feet in the twenty minutes after the flood and does not go down again inside the working day, and that rule is on a slate. **At about half past ten in the morning a man in a bell with a sheet of about four feet in an oilcloth fold in his inside pocket feels a thing in that trench answer the paper, and will not describe it in the boat until a man who could not hear out of one side of his head has been down and asked the same question.** The answer is entered in the second column at about six in the evening and in no other place: a paper cannot answer, whatever answered was answering a description, a record of a man holding a paper is not a record of the thing. **And on a flat stone about nine inches from the eleventh of eleven square-ended marks about three weeks old is a piece of worked lead about the size of a man's palm with nine notches in it, three of them deep, a place about the size of a thumb left out on purpose, no figure and no number — and the cut is the cut.** A man of about thirty-six named Corwin Tace, who says setting marks is what he does, puts it inside his coat and is not stopped.
10. **CHAPTER 460, FRIDAY THE TWENTY-SECOND. THE DISCLOSURE, THE BOUNDARY, TWO READ-BACKS, AND THE LAST OF THAT HARBOR'S STANDING CONDITION.** The holder of that writ tells Mara Venn, in his own mouth, before she is asked, what he did with the sheet and what answered it, and neither of them says he was right or wrong and it is in neither column. **What comes out of it is a printed boundary: the echo may inform a public record, and it may not decide anything this party does.** The sixth day of the hire is paid in coin on the deck. The fitting-out sheet is read back in full with both totals. The leaf is read back at about ten past five in the open, in the ship's own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, at one hundred and ninety-two, seven hundred and thirty-seven, none, one hundred and twenty-five at the hour and one hundred and ninety-three, seven hundred and thirty-nine, none, one hundred and twenty-five at the close, with both definitions on the face of the reading. Three people say one thing each about the water, the paper and the trip. The whole of that harbor's standing condition is on that page once and nowhere else.

### The four figures, and the fitting-out sheet

- **AT THE HOUR OF THE READING: ONE HUNDRED AND NINETY-TWO / EIGHT HUNDRED AND THIRTY-SEVEN / NONE / ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIVE. AT THE CLOSE OF THE DAY: ONE HUNDRED AND NINETY-THREE / EIGHT HUNDRED AND THIRTY-NINE / NONE / ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIVE.** The first column takes one entry a day and the day's own entry goes in after that day's reading; the second takes five a day, three before the hour and two after, and is not a count of anything anybody can check from a mole. The base of one hundred and eighty-three and seven hundred and eighty-nine at the close of Chapter 450 re-derives to one hundred and ninety-three and seven hundred and thirty-nine on these pages. **The third column is empty and unappointed, a boy of twenty-two's hand is at the head of it, and his surname is on no page of the ten. The fourth has taken no line in ten days, has no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it, is not closed and is not struck, and the reason it took no line was entered once, in the second column, at about ten past nine in the evening of the twenty-eighth day of August, and is entered again nowhere.**
- **THE FITTING-OUT SHEET. IN: FIVE THOUSAND SEVEN HUNDRED AND SIXTY, THREE HUNDRED AND TWENTY, ONE THOUSAND TWO HUNDRED AND EIGHTY, ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTY, TWO HUNDRED AND FORTY = SEVEN THOUSAND SEVEN HUNDRED AND SIXTY, BEING FORTY-EIGHT MARKS, SIX SHILLINGS AND EIGHTPENCE. OUT: NINETY-SIX, TWO HUNDRED AND FOUR, FOUR HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-SIX, ONE THOUSAND TWO HUNDRED AND FIFTY, SIX HUNDRED AND FORTY, SIX HUNDRED AND SEVENTY-TWO, ONE THOUSAND ONE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY, ONE THOUSAND THREE HUNDRED AND FORTY, ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTY-EIGHT, TWO HUNDRED AND FORTY-FOUR, SIX HUNDRED AND SEVENTY-TWO, TWO HUNDRED AND FIFTY = SEVEN THOUSAND TWO HUNDRED AND TWO, BEING FORTY-FIVE MARKS AND TWOPENCE. LEFT: FIVE HUNDRED AND FIFTY-EIGHT, BEING THREE MARKS, SIX SHILLINGS AND SIXPENCE.** By the close of the twentieth the out-column stood at six thousand two hundred and eighty, being thirty-nine marks, three shillings and fourpence. **The sheet carries no count of persons and has no figure on it for how many people are on it, and the count of eleven is on the Assembly's sheet in the room over a fish market and is on no other sheet in these ten chapters.**
- **THE BAG STANDS AT TWENTY-EIGHT PENCE, BEING TWO SHILLINGS AND FOURPENCE, ON ALL TEN DAYS, short of the wage of four marks, being six hundred and forty pence, by six hundred and twelve pence, being three marks eleven shillings, and it is never zero.** One hundred and sixty-eight in and one hundred and sixty-eight out on nine of the ten days, three hundred and thirty-six and three hundred and thirty-six on the sixteenth, for the whole of the ten days one thousand eight hundred and forty-eight pence in and one thousand eight hundred and forty-eight pence out, being eleven marks, seven shillings and fourpence each way, and twenty-eight plus one thousand eight hundred and forty-eight less one thousand eight hundred and forty-eight is twenty-eight. **The sixteenth is the only one of the ten that carried two days, because a berth fund paid that Saturday two days, and the count is nine times one hundred and sixty-eight, being one thousand five hundred and twelve, plus three hundred and thirty-six, being one thousand eight hundred and forty-eight. The figure keeps running on the days the holder of that writ is off the coast and the reason is in the second column: a berth fund pays a day for a day and does not care which coast the day happened on, and the two men at that berth are not the man who keeps the leaf.**

### The relationship pressure at the end of Chapter 460

- **Calder and Mara. THE COMMITTED RELATIONSHIP IS UNCHANGED AND UNTOUCHED AND NO WORD OF IT HAS BEEN SAID TWICE.** She is of no office, not on the crew, not restored, not forgiven, forty marks first after food standing whole. **She said no out loud on a quay on the seventeenth in front of thirty people and she was right, and he says so himself, and she did not forgive him for the pocket and did not thank him for the disclosure.** The boundary is hers and it is printed: the echo may inform a public record and it may not decide anything this party does. Her name is on two public sheets and is on no third.
- **Calder and the fitting-out sheet.** A man and a piece of paper, and the sheet says on its own face that it is a description of a made thing and not the thing it describes. **He carried it down the coast in an oilcloth fold in his inside pocket, he did not say so, it answered something, and he told her before she asked and it went into neither column.**
- **Calder and the eleven.** Nine people at four marks and two at one mark, and the nine are on a page with a name and an hour in their own hands, and six of them say out loud what the money was for and one of them said it was the flour money. **Nobody in that harbor is thanked for putting money in and nobody is going to be told the trip was worth it.**
- **Calder and the two who said no.** A master of about thirty-three on the thirteenth in a room over a fish market at about a quarter to five in the afternoon, and a woman of about thirty-one on the **fourteenth** in that shed at about four in the afternoon. Each gave a reason in her own mouth in front of other people, neither has been asked a second time on any of the days after it, and both refusals stand on the sheet at the same size as the figures.
- **Calder and Amos Trewin, of about twenty-nine.** He asked for the second descent and was given it, and the gasket went, and he came up with his left side about nine feet off, and he went on working that evening and the next four days, and nobody put a figure on it and nobody thanked him and nobody sent him home.
- **Calder and Corwin Tace, of about thirty-six.** A setter of marks with a tool roll and a warrant with a seal on it and no figure on it, about three weeks on that shelf, who says a warrant is a piece of paper that says somebody has paid for the coal. He is not a villain, not a general and not a face; he was asked one question about himself and none about the lead; he put the lead inside his coat and was not stopped.
- **Calder and Alden.** The far bench was occupied from ten until four on all ten days and the holder of that writ is in that harbor on two of them, and he did not go over to him on either. The four sentences of the ninth of October past are not repeated, not written down, and not followed by a fifth.

**Line Diver. NO STAGE WAS TAKEN IN THESE TEN CHAPTERS. THE COUNT OF *KEELWRIGHT* ACROSS THEM IS ZERO AND SO IS THE COUNT OF *CHORUS*. THE CHORUS DIVER STAGE IS NOT ENTERED AND IS NOT REHEARSED. THE FAULTREADER STAGE IS SPENT AND WAS NOT USED. NO ECHO WAS ENTERED BY ANYBODY, THE COUNT OF *ECHO* USED OF A SCENE A DIVER GOES INTO IS ZERO, NO PANEL WAS OPENED, AND NO CHAPTER OF THE TEN HAS A SCENE IN IT.** Every dive in the batch has a named tender on the surface and not in the boat, an independent line, a fixed air limit written as a figure, a reason with an hour against it before the diver goes down, and a cutoff the tender can pull without asking. What was paid instead of a power: a gasket at two hundred and forty-four pence, six thousand two hundred and eighty pence of material in ten days, coal at twice the figure at home, a hearing gone out of one side of a man of twenty-nine, and eleven people's money that is not coming back.

- **THE BAG IS TWENTY-EIGHT PENCE, BEING TWO SHILLINGS AND FOURPENCE, AGAINST A WAGE OF FOUR MARKS, BEING SIX HUNDRED AND FORTY PENCE, AND IT IS SHORT BY SIX HUNDRED AND TWELVE PENCE, BEING THREE MARKS ELEVEN SHILLINGS, AND IT IS NEVER ZERO. NOTHING HAS BEEN IN A TIN IN THAT SHED SINCE THE TWENTY-EIGHTH DAY OF APRIL PAST, AND NOT ONE PENNY OF THE VOYAGE'S COST CAME OUT OF THAT BAG, OUT OF THE OWNER OF ANY BOAT, OUT OF THE MAN WITH TWO PAPERS, OR OUT OF THE CROWN.**
- **THE WAGE COLUMN IS AT TWENTY-SIX LINES AND ONE HUNDRED AND FOUR MARKS WITH TWENTY ENVELOPES IN A CHEST, TWO WAGE TUESDAYS FELL IN THESE TEN DAYS, BEING THE FIFTY-FIRST ON THE TWELFTH OF OCTOBER PAST AND THE FIFTY-SECOND ON THE NINETEENTH, THE COLUMN DID NOT MOVE ON THE FIFTY-SECOND, AND FIFTY-TWO WEEKS STAND FALLEN DUE WITH NO ENVELOPE AGAINST ANY OF THEM.**
- **THE CISTERN WAS CHARGED THREE TIMES, BEING THE NINETIETH ON THE FOURTEENTH, THE NINETY-FIRST ON THE EIGHTEENTH AND THE NINETY-SECOND ON THE TWENTY-FIRST, AND WALKED ON BY NONE OF IT ON ANY OF THEM, AND THE TOP NAME ON THAT ROTA BOARD IS STILL OFF IT, AND THE OTHER SEVEN DAYS PUT NO CHARGE ON IT. THE WALL CAME DOWN BARE ONCE, BEING THE SEVENTY-SIXTH TIME ON THE SEVENTEENTH, AND WENT UP AT THE ANGLE IT HAS BEEN AT SINCE THE TWELFTH AND NOBODY PUT IT BACK.**
- **A HARBOR POORER ON THE TWENTY-SECOND DAY OF OCTOBER THAN ON THE THIRTEENTH, AND THE NEW POVERTY IS ELEVEN PEOPLE'S MONEY.** No flour and none coming this month, no barley since the middle of September, no barrel of lamp oil since the twenty-ninth day of August, a board at an end stall carrying four hundred and fifty pence with February's three hundred and seventy-eight above it and both dates on it and the figure of the first of June not taken down, physic at fourteen pence and none of it, the mole-head light out with its lens out since the seventh of May, the north berth out, the hose dead until the spring, the tide gang four men short, the hard at Ashtide unanswered, one berth short on the third lay, nineteen winters disputed. **The day-counts run on to one hundred and fifty-eight, one hundred and sixty, four hundred and ninety-eight, two hundred and sixty-four, eighty-two, thirty-seven, fifty-two, sixty-nine and a hundred, and every one of the nine was checked against its own base and against the day it stands on.**
- **STANDING UNPAID AND UNMOVED AND NONE OF IT ENTERED IN FULL IN THESE TEN DAYS: THREE MARKS TO A MAN OF ASHTIDE ON AN ANCHOR DATE THAT CAME IN ON THE ENTRY, RULED NOT RE-DATED; SEVEN PENCE TO THAT YARD'S OWN SHIPWRIGHT; EIGHT MARKS AND A DAY OF A BOAT TO THAT HARBOR'S OWN BELLWRIGHT, NOT ASKED; EIGHT SHILLINGS AND TENPENCE TO A WOMAN WITH HER NAME ON THE FIGURE; FORTY MARKS FIRST AFTER FOOD TO A PERSON OF NO OFFICE; FORTY MARKS WHOLE TO A BOY OF TWENTY-TWO, THE THREE NOTS A FIFTEENTH WEEK UNASKED FROM THE EIGHTEENTH OF OCTOBER; THE THIRD COLUMN UNFILLED AND UNAPPOINTED; A PAGE OF SIX NAMES ON A MOLE WITH A BOAT AS A PRICE AND A STONE IN ONE MAN'S OWN POCKET, SILENT FOR A HUNDRED DAYS; A MUNICIPAL CLAIM ON ONE OF THE THREE THINGS IN THE CIRCUIT CUSTODY ROOM; A BOX IN AN OFFICE OFF THE WEST BASIN THAT IS NOT EMPTY AND ANOTHER ON THE SAME TABLE THAT IS NOT EMPTY; A NINE-LINE SHEET WITH A SEAL ON IT IN THAT FRONT STREET FOR THE SIXTY-NINTH DAY; A CLAIM AGAINST THE COPY IN A BOOK AT A COUNTER OFF THE WEST BASIN, NOT WITHDRAWN; A LINE RULED UNDER A HEAD IN A PUBLIC VOLUME AND LEFT EMPTY; A ROPEMAKER OF ABOUT SIXTY-ONE WHO IS NOT IN HER ROOM; THE ELEVEN PEOPLE ON A PAPER OF FOUR LINES WHO HAVE BEEN TOLD NOTHING FURTHER; AND THE PLATE IN ELEVEN FEET, THE COMPARTMENT AND THE MANIFEST, NONE OF WHICH IS ON A PAGE OF THESE TEN CHAPTERS. NONE OF THE ABOVE IS PAID, ADVANCED, REDUCED OR IMPROVED ON ANY OF THE TEN DAYS.**

## Where the story is at the end of Chapter 440

### The movement's beats, in order, as they stand on the page

1. **CHAPTER 431, THURSDAY THE TWENTY-THIRD. THE EIGHTY-FOURTH CISTERN CHARGE, AND A BOAT ON THE FOUL.** One hundred and sixty-eight pence of oakum, iron, three-inch stuff, canvas and nails went out at about ten in the morning and one hundred and sixty-eight pence of a day's work at a berth came in at about four in the afternoon and the bag stands at five hundred and thirty-two pence where it stood at the open of the day. **A warp round a bollard parted at about two in the morning and a boat of about nineteen tons named the *Alewife* went up the foul off the south end with nobody in her.** Nine men unstepped and landed her mast in about fifty minutes and split a piece out of the mole coping; her wheel went into a boat; both anchors were let go and left in nine foot. Calder Marr packed the open garboard from the inside at about eleven foot and said out loud that it would hold until the flood. **The flood came at about twenty past six, set her beam ends in about four minutes, put her port rail against the mole's footing stones for about an hour and ten minutes, and at about half past seven she came off and took the ground on a bank four hundred yards down the foul in about nine foot.** Nobody was paid for that morning. Nessa Pike told the holder of that writ in the open that she has two figures in that harbor and none at all for a man in the water at four in the morning, and would not make one up, and that the person is the thing that costs and a day for a person has to be written on a paper and asked one man at a time.
2. **CHAPTER 432, FRIDAY THE TWENTY-FOURTH. THE NIGHT'S WINDOW, AND LOWFEN AS WORK.** A hundred and five minutes of ebb, about a quarter to four to about twenty past five. He went down in a bell off her starboard quarter and shored her with two baulks of oak; the boat came down about two inches and stopped dead. He found about nine feet of soft plank nine feet aft of the shore and put his thumb through the veneer of it about the size of a shilling and said that a shore does not stop soft plank. The pump leather went at about half past four and about fifty minutes of fresh water came over the side. **One hundred and sixty-eight pence went out at about nine in the morning.** **Ollum Trevask, of about thirty-four, of the second lay, who keeps the whole fouling ladder in that harbor in his own book and has never shown it to anybody, said out loud that they do not do it that way in Lowfen, where a man takes the mould off a piece of the old keel with the boat still floating in about two foot of water with two men on a pole and a third with the battens, and that the ground under a Lowfen hull is not the ground there next year because the reeds put it out and pull it back, and that a mould there is kept in a head and not in a book, and that he has never been to Lowfen in his life and that is how he knows.** A packet went down that coast at about four in the afternoon offering one day at the figure in chalk and telling whoever came, in the packet, that the figure being offered was not the figure anybody ought to take.
3. **CHAPTER 433, SATURDAY THE TWENTY-FIFTH. ELEVEN MASTERS, ONE AT A TIME, IN THE SAME WORDS.** The words were written at the head of the page before anybody was asked. Ten said yes and one said no. **Rowan Teel, of about fifty-one, of the second lay, whose right forearm is set out of his own hand, said no at about a quarter to six and gave his reason in his own mouth and said he would rather say it then than have somebody come to his door about it on the Tuesday; he was not asked again on any of the six days after it.** **Sedge Rundle, of about forty-six, out of Lowfen, said out loud that he goes by three things and none of them is on a paper.** One of the seven is Nessa Pike's own boat of about thirteen tons and she gave her hours and said the bill comes to her own table and not to anybody else's. A woman of about fifty-eight with an end stall said the figure on that page is her figure, that she wrote it up in chalk on the first of June, and that she is not going to be told what to do with it. One hundred and sixty-eight pence came in and the bag stands at five hundred and thirty-two.
4. **CHAPTER 434, SUNDAY THE TWENTY-SIXTH. A TWELFTH WEEK, AND A BELLWRIGHT OFF THE REEF LINE.** The three nots of the eighth of June past stand in the first day of a twelfth week unasked. **Mina Kett, of about thirty-four, a bellwright of Tidewatch, came down at about half past ten with her own tools in a box and took eleven battens off the keel of a boat of about nineteen tons lying on that hard since June in about two hours and ten minutes, and numbered the ends in pencil with her own marks and not with figures.** She was told she would be paid at the figure in chalk and **said out loud once that that is a caulker's figure and not hers, that a bellwright off that line gets five shillings, being sixty pence, and that she has been getting that for nine years and has never asked anybody for more, and that she was saying it once so that it would be in somebody's head and was not going to say it again and was not going to be thanked for it.** The room over a joiner's shop was let out at two o'clock; about twenty went up and three came down and eleven of the twenty could not read; Hobb Lee read the head-notes out loud with his own name and the hour under each; there was no claim in any of them. **About forty pieces of lead came out of the lid of her box at about four o'clock and the nail in the door frame of her workshop and the woman of about sixty-one and the penny and the twenty-six years are on the page, and she said these are not for this coast and are not to go on a wall.** Two baulks of oak planed went out at one hundred and sixty-eight pence and the bag stands at three hundred and sixty-four.
5. **CHAPTER 435, MONDAY THE TWENTY-SEVENTH. THE SEVENTY-THIRD WIPE, THE EIGHTY-FIFTH CISTERN, AND THE CUTOFF.** The wall came down bare for the seventy-third time and went up at the angle it has been at since the twelfth and nobody put it back; the cistern was charged and walked on for the eighty-fifth time and the top name on that rota board is still off it. A sheet of good paper came from the counter in a room off that market at about nine in the morning at a penny out of the holder's own coat and not out of that bag, with four days on it and one figure on it. **Mara Venn said one thing about it: that it has got a person in it, that there is no column in that yard's book for a person who has been asked to turn up, and that she would put it in the second column with the hour against it and not in the first.** **Halvard Ness, of about twenty-three, laid fifteen fathoms of chain off his tender's quarter round a spurle and back with a weight on the tail of it, and said he would not ask anybody's leave to pull it and that nobody in that boat had any standing to tell him not to.** The woman of fifty-eight was told that the figure on her slate is the same figure as the charge at the foot of the sheet on the wall of her stall, and said it has been the same figure since the first of June and that two figures on two pieces of wood nine feet apart is no more than that, and asked for her tobacco to be paid for. One hundred and sixty-eight pence came in and the bag stands at five hundred and thirty-two.
6. **CHAPTER 436, TUESDAY THE TWENTY-EIGHTH. THE FORTY-NINTH WAGE TUESDAY, AND A BOAT THAT STRUCK A BAULK.** The column did not move; forty-nine weeks stand fallen due at the close of the day. Seven boats and about thirty men were on the water from ten past seven until the last of the ebb. **The new piece of keel came off the battens in three pieces and did not fit, and nobody in that company said a word about it for about ten minutes, and then Mina Kett put her thumb into the end of the middle piece and said out loud to about thirty men that it is a guess with a curve in it and that she had told them so; a sixteenth was taken off the whole length and not off one end and it went on in about two hours.** The chain weight came over the rail at twenty-two minutes past two and the reason was written down with the hour against it. **At about ten past two a boat of about twenty-two tons struck a baulk of oak that that yard's own hands had laid down at half past eight in the morning with about nine inches of it out of the water in a sea and no light on it and no flag and nothing on it, and opened about nine foot of her garboard and put a hole in her lee rail about the size of two hands, and nobody was hurt.** The owner said in his own mouth that the baulk is that yard's and the bill is that yard's. Two payments of one hundred and sixty-eight pence, being three hundred and thirty-six pence, went out and one hundred and sixty-eight came in and the bag stands at three hundred and sixty-four.
7. **CHAPTER 437, WEDNESDAY THE TWENTY-NINTH. THE BILL, AND THE SECOND MAN IN THAT BELL.** A caulker of about twenty-three who crews in no boat and holds no office and is on no sheet was asked in that shed whether he would take the caulking of that joint on that afternoon and said the figure he works to out loud before he was asked for the day. **A man of about twenty-nine of the third lay went down in that bell at about half past five in the morning, one at a time, and came up and said there is a hole about two foot aft of where the shore is, and that it is not open, and that it is soft, and that his hand went in about the depth of a thumb and came back with a smell off it that was not tar and was not oil, and that he has not been in her in June and is not going to give anybody anything else.** The first man said he had put his thumb through the veneer of that plank on the Friday before last. **Both accounts are in the book and neither agrees with the other.** The plank and iron and roves and copper went out at one hundred and sixty-eight pence and the bag stands at one hundred and ninety-six.
8. **CHAPTER 438, THURSDAY THE THIRTIETH. THE EIGHTY-SIXTH CISTERN, AND A WORD ASKED FOR OUT LOUD.** The third and last charge in these ten days and the top name is still off that board. **The reason a man was put in that bell was written down before he went down, which had not been done before.** A master of about forty-six out of Lowfen went down and said the plank is not soft and is as sound as anything in her and that he put his whole hand flat on it and did not try to force it, and said that he is not going to change it because somebody else had been in there and he had not, and that one of the three men is wrong and he does not know which. **Hobb Lee came down that slip at about eleven in the morning in daylight and asked what the man who keeps a keel right in between tides with a chain and a weight on it is called, and was told there is a word and it is not taken by being said, and said he would not ask again and would not say it at his table and that he would not read it out in that room.** The woman of fifty-eight said three days had gone by and not one penny of any of it had come off anybody's boat and would like that written down somewhere and not on her slate. One hundred and sixty-eight pence came in and the bag stands at three hundred and sixty-four.

FOUR REQUESTS AND THE SAME NINE WORDS, AND THE WORD SAID OUT LOUD.** **A man of about forty-four asked for a line to be struck out of a sheet carrying his name and an hour and eleven minutes of lateness, and was refused. A bellwright of about thirty-four asked for her line to be struck out of the same sheet on the ground that the figure on it is not hers and that a man of about forty-six who cannot read could be told in three weeks that a bellwright is paid a mark and eightpence in Morrow Quay, and was refused, and asked for a second line under it and got one, and that line is in the second column and names her own figure of five shillings, being sixty pence, and the hundred and eight pence a day she is under by. THE READ-BACK, THE FIGURES, AND THE STANDING CONDITION.** The leaf was read back at about ten past five in the evening on the flat of the bench stone at that mole head, in the open, in the ship's own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, **with both definitions on the face of that reading: one hundred and seventy-two at the hour and one hundred and seventy-three at the close; seven hundred and thirty-seven at the hour and seven hundred and thirty-nine at the close; none; one hundred and twenty-five at the hour and one hundred and twenty-five at the close, with no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it, the column not closed and not struck out, and the reason entered once on the twenty-eighth of August and entered again nowhere.** **A caulker of about twenty-three was paid one hundred and sixty-eight pence in coin on the flat of the bench stone at about four in the afternoon, asked for by name at about ten in the morning on Wednesday the twenty-ninth of September past, and on no other day of these ten.** The room over a joiner's shop was let out for the fifth time and about seventeen went up and three came down, and about twenty went up on the twenty-sixth, which is about thirty-seven across the two Sundays. **The woman of no office said one thing four feet off the stone: that what is hers and what is anybody's has to be written down and is not that yard's book, that the four columns and the figure and the method do not go on the table in Fish Street or on any wall in this harbor, that her name does not go on a sheet for any of this, and that forty marks first after food is not reduced by a chain and a weight and a bellwright from off the reef line.** The bag is one hundred and ninety-six pence, being one mark and three shillings, against a wage of six hundred and forty, and is short by four hundred and forty-four pence, being two marks ten shillings and fourpence. **A harbor poorer on the second day of October than on the twenty-third day of September and poorer than on the fourteenth day of May.**

### The movement's beats, in order, as they stand on the page

1. **CHAPTER 421, MONDAY THE THIRTEENTH. THE SEVENTY-FIRST WIPE, THE EIGHTY-FIRST CISTERN, AND THE MAN WHO CANNOT READ.** A day at a berth came in at one hundred and sixty-eight pence and the bag is five hundred and seventy-six pence, being three marks eight shillings. **Emmet Slade, of about thirty, of that lay, with a boat of about nine tons and a claim window on a wreck off the point, came up that slip at about two in the afternoon, said he had heard there was a paper against him, said in the first half minute that he cannot read, and was told there is a paper at a counter in an office off the west basin, that nobody in that shed has seen it, that it cannot be read to him there because he would have the reader's head and not the paper, and that nobody in that shed knows whether it is against his boat.** He was told that being told it is not would be a kindness and not a finding, and he said he would go the next day. **And at about four a screw-steam packet put her hook on and a man of about thirty-four landed a sack of printed sheets at a stall and said out loud that the lot had been given to him at the top of a gangway by a man behind a counter with a book open who did not ask his name.**
2. **CHAPTER 422, TUESDAY THE FOURTEENTH. THE FORTY-SEVENTH WAGE TUESDAY, A MESSAGE OUT OF A BOY'S HAND, AND TWENTY-FOUR SHEETS THROUGH A COUNTER.** The column is at twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks with twenty empty envelopes folded the same way by a woman of about fifty-eight about eleven weeks ago, and it did not move. **Dill Cardew, of about seventeen, carried a message ashore down the slip at the second lay and a man of about forty-four off the water with two fingers of his left hand stiff took it out of his hand, read it standing up in about the time it takes to read four lines, said it was a thing a man does not carry in a street, put it inside his coat and went up the slip.** What the boy lost was the paper and the hour he was going to be somewhere else in, and he stood on a step for about twenty-five minutes with no reason in his hand. The man he was going to did not send it again. **Twenty-four sheets went through a copyist's counter in a room off that market at a penny a sheet, being twenty-four pence, being two shillings, out of a stall-holder's hand, and the woman of about fifty-nine did not ask what she was copying and was not asked and did not stop.**
3. **CHAPTER 423, WEDNESDAY THE FIFTEENTH. THE NOTICE, PRINTED IN FULL, AND THE FIGURE IT IS PUT UP ON.** The sheet went up at about ten in the morning on the outside of the oil slate, and the oil figure was not taken down first and cannot be taken off. **Its first line says that a piece of worked glass that has had a scene taken from a living person keeps what the scene was, and that what the scene was stands off the piece into the air of a room and settles on the people in that room and is taken home in the clothes; its second says it is not a fever and not a disease and will sit in a market the same as it sits in a room; its third says every person who has been in a room with such a piece is to be entered in the claim book at the counter of the harbor authority of the town where he stands; its fourth says a book is not a court; its fifth says no person and no town is named and that it is put up on the outside of this figure; and its sixth gives the charge for lodging one claim as one hundred and sixty-eight pence, being one mark and eightpence, and says a claim so lodged is read out in the room where the public book is kept, on a Sunday, by a man at the end of the table.** The man of about thirty-four said he could not say it was a lie. **The woman of about fifty-eight turned her slate about so the oil figure was showing again, moved the sack off her counter against her own back boards, and said the figure is not coming off for a piece of paper with a date on the top of it.** About thirty people stood in front of that wall by noon and nobody put a hand on it. **Calder Marr read it twice, found no name in it and no town in it, stood in front of the date at the head of it, and did not go up the hill.**
4. **CHAPTER 424, THURSDAY THE SIXTEENTH. THE EIGHTY-SECOND CISTERN, THE CAULKER'S SEVENTH DAY, AND THE SIX LINES READ ALOUD.** A man of about forty-six read the six lines out loud in the middle aisle at about eleven in front of about thirty people of whom about nine could not read, and wrote his own name and the hour under it on the back of a crate. Four men said out loud they had been in the room on the twelfth, and there were about twenty people in that room and nobody counted who was in it. A man of about thirty-six said he had been in a shed with glass off a wreck in April and had come out and eaten his supper, and a man of about forty-one said he has not been near a piece since the fourth of June and has had a cold in his teeth since about three o'clock on the Sunday, and said out loud that he does not know which of two things is the thing that does it. **And Hobb Lee said out loud that he will not read a claim out at that table as a claim, and gave his reason twice, and said that the day he does he has turned that table into a court with a net-mender at the head of it.**
5. **CHAPTER 425, FRIDAY THE SEVENTEENTH. THE COUNTER SHUT AND THE PAPER ON THE WEST BASIN.** A chandler of about fifty whose wife keeps the count would not sell eight fathoms of tarred rope at four shillings, being forty-eight pence, to **Nate Pry, of about forty-four, of that lay, who carried a piece of worked glass about two hands square out of a boat's hold in June on his own back for a shilling and a half and has not been near a piece since**, and gave his reason in his own mouth: he is not going to stand in his shop and ask a man whether he has been in a room with a piece of glass, and he has a wife and a girl of eleven behind that counter, and he would rather be wrong about himself than about her. He took fourpence on an old account and gave the rope back onto the man's arm. **And at about four in the afternoon a man of about fifty, who works at a table with two papers on it in an office off the west basin, put a four-line paper on that counter with no name on it and no seal at the foot of it, saying a claim has been entered under a sheet that went up in the front street on the fifteenth, that a person who has been in a room with a piece of worked glass with a scene in it is to be entered in the claim book of that harbor under his own name, and that until he has been entered a claim window held by him is held.**
6. **CHAPTER 426, SATURDAY THE EIGHTEENTH. THE BERTH HELD, AND THE WORD *OFF*.** A sheet tied to the peg of a berth at the head of the third lay with a piece of line, dated the seventeenth, held a boat of about thirteen tons and no papers, and her owner said the sixth clause lets me in and does not give me a berth, and put her on the hard at the back of that lay from about seven until about ten and went out on the sixth clause that evening and came in past the outer marks at about five the next morning. **And Emmet Slade, who cannot read, was at a counter in an office off the west basin at about eleven with his name written at the top of a sheet, and was told that the word on it is off, and said that off is a different word to held, and was told that off is the word that is on the paper and that he was not going to be given another one; and asked whether it was against his boat and was told his boat is not on that counter.** A man of about thirty-one with a chart in a bag said one sentence at the foot of a slip and said he is not on a sheet and is not going to be.
7. **CHAPTER 427, SUNDAY THE NINETEENTH. THE ROPEMAKER IS FOUND OUT AND PUT OUT OF HER ROOM.** A man of about twenty-six who stacks empties said on the Friday before last at a quay, to about four people, that the woman who carried a box up two flights of stairs on the Sunday before lives on the third lay; nobody asked him where he got it. **At about eleven in the morning Ruben Priest, of about fifty-eight, who takes the rents in two houses on that slip and has taken this one for eleven years at nine marks a year, being one thousand four hundred and forty pence, paid out of rope, told her the room is not hers after the end of the quarter.** He gave his reason in his own mouth and asked her nothing, and said he was not going to ask because an answer given in a street stays in the head of the man who asked for it. She asked him one question, which was when. She cut the rope off her box at about one o'clock, lifted the panel out and put it back in, knotted the rope the way she knots it, and carried the box down the slip on her own bad knee backwards with the barrow's wheel against the step above her between one o'clock and half past two, and nobody on that lay carried anything for her. **The room over the joiner's shop was let out for the third time the same afternoon, about sixteen went up and three came down, eleven of the sixteen could not read, nine heads were read out loud from about two minutes past two to about twenty-one minutes past three, there was no claim in any of the nine and no claim on that table, and the woman of about fifty-eight came up with her slate and said out loud that a sheet on a wall is not on that table and that she is not going to ask anybody to read it out in there.**
8. **CHAPTER 428, MONDAY THE TWENTIETH. THE SEVENTY-SECOND WIPE, THE EIGHTY-THIRD CISTERN, A DATE THAT ENDED, AND THE DIVER.** **The fourth line of the paper at the top left of that door in Fish Street ended on the said day and that paper has been on that door twenty days and has been answered by nobody**, and about sixteen people went up that stair on the Sunday before and whether one of the eleven was in that room is not a thing anybody in that room looked for. **A man went down in a bell at about eleven foot at a berth on the third lay at ten in the morning with nine foot of a crate of three pieces of worked glass off his left shoulder, put a mend in a garboard with oakum and a marlinspike, and came up at about twenty past eleven.** He sat on the stones and said three things and no more, and said that he has had that taste of iron three times in nine months and that on each of those three times he was within a foot of a piece of worked glass for about as long as it takes to boil an egg, and that he has got no reading out of it and is not going to say that he has. **The ship's hand said out loud that she has got no figure for that and is not going to invent one, and wrote one line in the second column against a reason with no name against it.**
9. **CHAPTER 429, TUESDAY THE TWENTY-FIRST. THE FORTY-EIGHTH WAGE TUESDAY, AND THE BOY TELLS HIM TWICE AND WRONG.** Forty-four pence went out for a loaf and a half, a candle and a pot, and the bag is five hundred and thirty-two pence, being three marks four shillings and fourpence. **A boy of about seventeen was sent by a man behind a counter in that market to tell Emmet Slade that his window is stopped and that he is to hand in a third of anything landed, and told him in about eight words in the middle of that slip; and he said out loud that there is no third of anything, and that he has now got it twice and both times a bit different, and that the next market was the following morning, and he went home and did not take his boat out.** Nobody in that yard asked that boy where he was on the fourteenth. **And at about half past nine in the evening the holder of that writ said out loud, once, in a working man's own account of what he wrote down on the twenty-second day of August past and why, that he wrote eleven dates on a leaf of his own hand in a room over a fish market, in the order he read them, off a board about a yard wide, with no name and no figure against any of the eleven, and that he did it because in July he had a thing only he had and in August two other men had things only they had, and that he is not going to tell anybody what is on it unless it is read out in that room on a Sunday with his name and the hour under it.**
10. **CHAPTER 430, WEDNESDAY THE TWENTY-SECOND. THE READ-BACK, THE FIGURES, AND THE STANDING CONDITION.** The leaf was read back at about ten past five in the evening on the flat of the bench stone at that mole head, in the open, in the ship's own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, **with both definitions on the face of that reading: one hundred and sixty-two at the hour and one hundred and sixty-three at the close; six hundred and eighty-seven at the hour and six hundred and eighty-nine at the close; none; one hundred and twenty-five at the hour and one hundred and twenty-five at the close, with no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it, the column not closed and not struck out, and the reason entered once on the twenty-eighth of August and entered again nowhere.** The woman of no office said one thing four feet off the stone and was not answered and was not improved on. The bag is five hundred and thirty-two pence against a wage of six hundred and forty and is short by one hundred and eight pence, being nine shillings. **There is no flour in that market, there has been no barrel of lamp oil in that harbor since the twenty-ninth day of August, the figure of four hundred and fifty pence is on a board that is not cleared with the new sheet on the same square of wall above it, the paper of four lines in Fish Street is on that door and has been answered by nobody, the nine-line sheet with a seal on it is on the front street wall for thirty-nine days, the light is out, the north berth is out, the hose is dead until the spring, the tide gang is four men short, the hard at Ashtide is unanswered, one berth on the third lay is short, nineteen winters are disputed, and forty-eight weeks stand fallen due with no envelope against any of them. A harbor is poorer on the twenty-second day of September than on the thirteenth and poorer than on the fourteenth of May.**

### The four figures at the close of Chapter 430, and which definition each is

- **AT THE HOUR OF THE READING: ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTY-TWO / SIX HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-SEVEN / NONE / ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIVE. AT THE CLOSE OF THE DAY: ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTY-THREE / SIX HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-NINE / NONE / ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIVE.**
- **THE FIRST COLUMN'S FIGURE IS A COUNT OF ENTRIES AND THE FOURTH'S IS A COUNT OF LINES, AND A DAY OF THE FIRST COLUMN CARRIES ONE ENTRY AGAINST IT WHATEVER ELSE THAT DAY PRINTED, SO THAT A STRANGER WITH A LEAF AND A PENCIL CAN COUNT BOTH. THE SECOND COLUMN'S FIGURE IS THAT LEDGER'S OWN AND IS NOT A COUNT OF ANYTHING A STRANGER CAN CHECK FROM A MOLE.** Both definitions are on the face of Chapter 430's own reading, in the ship's mouth, and the thirty-day run is re-derived from the close of Chapter 400: the first column's base is one hundred and thirty-three and takes one entry against each of the thirty days with no day in two of them; the second column's base is five hundred and thirty-nine and takes five a day, three before the hour of that day's reading and two after it; the third takes none and nobody is appointed to it; **the fourth takes no line in this volume and stands where it stands.**
- **THE THINGS THAT CAME OFF THE PANEL AND THE THINGS THAT CAME OFF THE CRATE ARE THE FIGURES OF THIS MOVEMENT AND NEITHER OF THEM IS IN THAT LEDGER.** A cold in the teeth and a taste of iron like a nail and a man not knowing which of two doors he came out of; and the same three things in a man in a bell who could not tell which of two hatches he came up out of. And, out of a mouth and not out of a paper: a date at the head of a notice, a charge at the foot of it, a figure on a board that did not come down, and a sack standing against the back boards of an end stall with a stone on it.

### What is owed and what is not

**OWED TO THE BOOK BY A LATER MOVEMENT OF THIS VOLUME AND NOT BY THIS BATCH: the sheet of six lines on the wall at the back of that end stall is a Crown claim and it is not withdrawn and it is not going to be, and the crisis it made is not undone and none of the five costs is given back, and a later movement may not knock it down and may not print the date at the head of it out loud beside anything;** the fourth box in an office off the west basin is still empty and something is still to go into it in this volume against the wish of the man of about fifty and nobody in that yard is to ask him about it; the partial confession of a man of sixty-one is this volume's and comes down to the shed in four sentences and is not in these ten chapters; the far bench keeps its one shoe; **THE SEVEN AGAINST THE ONE MUST STILL BE ACCOUNTED FOR ON THE FACE OF A PAGE BY MOVEMENT 5**; the copyist of about fifty-nine is not to be asked again and what she is copying is not to be produced, read out or named without her asking, and twenty-four sheets went through that counter on the fourteenth and she was not asked and did not stop; Peat Marrow is not to be paid and not to be thanked for five afternoons at a wall and is not to be put on a list; **the movement's own reversal is on the page in two halves and NOBODY IS TO SAY OUT LOUD THAT ONE HALF IS THE ANSWER TO THE OTHER, AND NOBODY IS TO PRINT THE EIGHTH OF MAY BESIDE THE ELEVEN DATES ON ANY PAGE, IN ANY ROOM OR IN ANY CONVERSATION**; the twelve-term sweep, the declaration-of-absence sweep, the weekday sweep, the money-gloss sweep, the quote-parity sweep and the separation sweep for the date must all be run again by the phase that writes the next batch and by the volume close, on bodies, on every ledger column, on the daily apparatus and on the closing block; and the day-counts below run on one a day and nothing turns on a round figure.

**NOT OWED AND NOT TO BE RESTARTED:** the hundred and twenty-sixth line in that ledger, which nobody is to enter in this volume; a hundred and seventy-first day of the ninety; a forty-ninth wage Tuesday paid; a second loss of flour; the third of the three things in that room and the claim on it, which is not withdrawn and which nobody is going to ask to have withdrawn; the name of the office at the foot of that first paper's seal line out loud, which is Movement 5's and is said once by a working man reading the foot of a paper out loud in a room; the title of the charter, which is in no mouth before the last movement; the bellwright of that harbor, who is not asked; Sera Mott, who is not asked again; the plate at the fifth seam, in eleven feet, with its note open, not looked at, not measured, not touched, not asked about and not named; the first echo's witness, who stays where he is; and the eleven people on that paper, who are to be told nothing further by anybody in that harbor and are to read it on that door with their own eyes in their own time.

1. **CHAPTER 411, FRIDAY THE THIRD. THE BOOK, THE ROOM, THE HEAD-RULE, AND A PAPER ON THE DOOR.** A room over a joiner's shop at the top of Fish Street with a long table in it, four benches and a lamp on a nail, no board on the wall, no list, no name over the door, let out on a Sunday by a man of about thirty-four who carries a bowl down to the step at two and takes it in at six and does not ask who is going in. The book is bound in a re-backed canvas about two inches thick, was begun on the twentieth of April past, and carries **thirty heads on the said day**. Its head is five lines: four lines to be filled under every head, being what the thing is, where it came from, who stands where it is, and what it does not show; the refusals are on it and are not smaller than the rest; nothing entered in it is a decision and nothing binds anybody and a man's no goes in with the reason against his name and his name as plainly as a yes; head-notes are read out on a Sunday with the reader's name and the hour in his own hand on the day. **The second line of that head has been rubbed at the end for about forty years of an elbow on a table and the man who keeps the room declined to say why, because the first year is not this year and is not his telling.** Four people read the volume through from the first page to the last, being the holder of that writ, a woman of no office, a man of about forty-six who mends nets, and at about half past six a man of about twenty-six who stacks empties. A count of eleven people who cannot read was arrived at that day by two people counting separately and adding: **six by the woman of about fifty-eight in her own trade, five by the man of about twenty-six on the quay, and six and five is eleven.** The reader said out loud that on a Sunday he will read every head-note off that table and write his own name and the hour under each in his own hand on the day, and that he is a man of forty-six and does not charge a room for reading to a man who cannot read. And at the top left of that door there is a paper with four lines on it, under a drawing-pin and a fold of oiled paper, which is not the notice of the seventeenth of May past.

The room holds a table, two benches and a lamp on a nail and has no cupboard, no chest, no shelves and no box in it, so nothing of any size was put down and taken out again in four minutes. **He has the eleven written down in his own hand in his coat in the order he asked them in and has shown them to nobody and has not destroyed them, and has been asked twice to take the paper down and has not.** He said the whole of that paper is a date at the end of the fourth line, and a name on a door is a different kind of thing from a date on a door and cannot be taken off again.

He said a dash is true and a dash is a hole and that he has known it was a hole since the eighteenth of June and has not come back to it in eighty days, and that he has never once gone down that volume with a pencil and counted what was in the fourth line of each head, and that a man who has not looked does not get to tell a man who has looked what is there.**

He wrote it in four lines in pencil on the inside of the back cover with his own name and the date, and said that he was not in that room on the eighteenth of June and is not going to say who was, and that four people stood in that room while he said it and not one of the four put the question to him.** The holder of that writ asked one thing in the passage, in about six words, and Ned Vaile said it was true, and the holder of that writ said that he had read that head on Friday the third and put his thumb on the third line and left the volume shut on that table and had not counted anything, and **then neither of them said one word about it, and they went down the hill together and neither of them said one word about it.**

### The four figures at the close of Chapter 420, and which definition each is

- **AT THE HOUR OF THE READING: ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTY-TWO / SIX HUNDRED AND THIRTY-SEVEN / NONE / ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIVE. AT THE CLOSE OF THE DAY: ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTY-THREE / SIX HUNDRED AND THIRTY-NINE / NONE / ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIVE.**
- **THE FIRST COLUMN'S FIGURE IS A COUNT OF ENTRIES AND THE FOURTH'S IS A COUNT OF LINES, AND A DAY OF THE FIRST COLUMN CARRIES ONE ENTRY AGAINST IT WHATEVER ELSE THAT DAY PRINTED, SO THAT A STRANGER WITH A LEAF AND A PENCIL CAN COUNT BOTH. THE SECOND COLUMN'S FIGURE IS THAT LEDGER'S OWN AND IS NOT A COUNT OF ANYTHING A STRANGER CAN CHECK FROM A MOLE.** Both definitions are on the face of Chapter 420's own reading, in the ship's mouth, and the twenty-day run is re-derived from the close of Chapter 400: the first column's base is one hundred and thirty-three and takes one entry against each of the twenty days with no day in two of them; the second column's base is five hundred and thirty-nine and takes five a day, three before the hour of that day's reading and two after it; the third takes none and nobody is appointed to it; **the fourth takes no line in this volume and stands where it stands.**
- **THE FOUR THINGS THAT CAME OFF THE PANEL IN THAT ROOM, AND THE ONE THING THAT CAME OFF THE PAGE, ARE THE FIGURES OF THIS MOVEMENT AND NEITHER OF THEM IS IN THAT LEDGER.** Thirty-one heads, thirty with four lines and one with three; a dash at the end of the third line of the twenty-second; and the second line of that head rubbed at the end for forty years and not said. And, out of a mouth and not out of a paper, a cold in the teeth and a taste of iron like a nail and a man not knowing which of two doors he came out of.

### The relationship pressure at the end of Chapter 420

- **Calder and Mara. She read the second line of that head twice in Chapter 411 and said somebody has had their arm on that page for a very long time. She put forty pence of her own into the bowl on the step out of her own hand and did not say why and was not asked. **She was not in that room on the twelfth and did not come up that slip at any hour of that day, and the thing in the box in the back room of a house on the third lay is not hers and is not to be asked about by her, and neither woman nor man is to be asked for the other half of what came off the thing on the hill.** The two halves carried off the fragment on the twenty-fourth of August have not been matched and are not going to be.

## Where the story is at the end of Chapter 410

### The movement's beats, in order, as they stand on the page

1. **CHAPTER 401, TUESDAY THE TWENTY-FOURTH, THE FORTY-FOURTH WAGE TUESDAY. THE KNOCK.** He went up the hill at twenty to ten with his hands empty and knocked on a shut door in a corridor where, on the evening of Monday the twenty-third of August, he had stood and read nine lines twice and had not knocked. The door was opened by Saul Drury, a copying clerk of that office, about forty, who said nothing and left the door standing open. The hour ran from ten until about twenty to eleven, and the clerk was in the room the whole of it and put a lamp on a table without being asked and stood six feet off and said the hour in five words. The thing on the far shelf is about nine inches by six and its edge over nine inches is cut and not broken and the arris is still on it. It has a seam across it at about a third of the way up. **THE HOLDER SAID THAT A SEAM IS WHERE ONE MAKER'S PRESSURE MET ANOTHER'S AND NEITHER WON ALL THE WAY, AND THAT IT IS THE ONLY HONEST MARK IN RECOVERED WORK, AND THAT IT SAYS TWO PEOPLE MADE IT AND BOTH OF THEM WERE FRIGHTENED, AND THAT HE CANNOT SAY WHICH OF THE TWO WAS IN THE ROOM IT WAS CUT IN.** The woman of no office said that was not an answer; he said it was the only one he had. It went back on the far shelf on the same place under the same number. **The middle shelf was between the door and the far wall on the way in and on the way out and the holder did not turn his head at it or at the claim book above it and the clerk did not turn his either.** A request for another hour of the same thing was made in the corridor at about ten past eleven and refused in a clerk's nine words.
2. **THE AFTERTASTE, AND IT IS A REAL THING AND NOT A DISEASE.** The holder came out of the room with a window at about the height of his head, a board across the outside of it, a line of daylight under the board that does not move, water about four feet down going the other way and a man's hand on it going fast and **not frightened**. The woman of no office came out with a smell of tar and a hot iron and something under it she has no name for, and a woman counting in the dark and not losing her place and going to the end anyway. **They have the hand and the counting and neither of them can put them together, and on Sunday the twenty-ninth they agreed in their own mouths to stop and not to try to match them, because the day one of them matches them by guessing is the day one of them is wrong for the rest of their lives.** That agreement is the whole of what the aftertaste does to the plot in this movement and it is not a disease and not a fever and not glass and it is told out of two bodies and not out of a paper.
3. **CHAPTER 402, WEDNESDAY THE TWENTY-FOURTH'S NEXT DAY. THE REFUSAL ON THE DOOR, IN THE CLERK'S HAND.** Four lines, no seal, no office, the clerk's own name and the word *clerk* after it, and it says a second paper will be on that door on the second of September and not on any day before it. The holder identified the hand from a line the same man had ruled with a flat rule at about ten past ten on the Tuesday. The woman of no office did not go up the hill again and said on the mole that the thing she is carrying is not sitting still and that she would not say the other half of it.
4. **CHAPTERS 403 TO 409. THE RETURN, AND THE COUNT, AND THE MAN WHO COUNTED IT.** A sheet about two foot by three is nailed to nine feet of wall inside the door of the office on the west basin. It is the return of recovered glass entered at that harbor since the first of April, ruled in five blocks by month, with a line for every day and a figure in the right-hand column on a day a thing came in and a single stroke across the line on a day nothing did, and a space two inches deep at the foot with the word *carried* over it and nothing in it. Five small figures in the hand of a clerk of about sixty stand at the head of the five blocks and are the number of lines in each block that carry a figure. **A man of about fifty-three with a bad back, Peat Marrow, who works a winch on the third lay, counted the five blocks on five afternoons, one at a time, with a stub of pencil on the flat of his own left hand, on his own time, and was not paid for it and was not thanked for it and said it once in a front street on a day he had named in advance.** The count: **one hundred and forty-five lines, one hundred and sixteen carrying a figure, twenty-nine struck across, and the summands seventy-one, ninety-six, seventy-nine, eighty-eight and fifty-seven, which is three hundred and ninety-one.** He counted the lines of the first and second blocks twice and the other three once and added each of the hundred and sixteen figures exactly once, and gave the reason for not going over the figures again, which is that he was not going to start wanting it to be a different number. On the first of September the figure went into the first column of that yard's own leaf in the holder's hand with the five summands and the line count under it and no name against it, and was read out in that shed at about ten past four with the hour against it.
5. **CHAPTERS 403 TO 409. THE YARD'S MONEY, AND THE MAN OF FIFTY-EIGHT'S SLATE.** Three days at a berth came in and two days of a caulker and a loaf and a half and a candle and a pot went out, and the bag stands at two hundred and eighty-four pence. A woman of about fifty-eight put her slate on the bench stone face up on the Friday and said that six men asked her what it costs to be in a boat of that yard's for a day and that one of them, who is fifty-one and has a boat called the *Anna Ray* of about fifty tons and is owed nineteen winters, said he would not do it for that, and that she said good to him. On the Saturday a man of about forty-four with a shop on the far street asked in the middle aisle of that market how many pieces of recovered glass have been landed and entered at that harbor, and was told that there was not a figure, and that if there was one it was not going on anything and not going in that front street and not going on the wall in that other street.
6. **CHAPTER 405, SATURDAY THE TWENTY-EIGHTH. THE REASON, ENTERED ONCE.** In that shed, in the yard's own mouth: the yard's time went into the first column and into a convoy and into a caulker's day; the fourth column is a page no man can check; and there was a man on the flat of the bench stone at four in the morning on the Friday who had to be paid first and was paid before anybody in that yard put a word down about what a thing is not. **THE FOURTH COLUMN THEREFORE TOOK NO LINE IN ANY OF THESE TEN DAYS AND THERE IS NO HUNDRED AND TWENTY-SIXTH LINE IN IT AND THE COLUMN IS NOT CLOSED AND IS NOT A STRIKE-OUT AND NOBODY HAS CLOSED IT.** Every later ledger carries the fact that the reason has been entered and does not enter it again.
7. **CHAPTERS 406 TO 409. THE PEOPLE, EACH ON A PAGE AND ON A DAY.** Isaac Fell, a caulker of about twenty-three, asked for by name on the Wednesday for the Friday and on the Saturday for the Tuesday, and paid in coin on the flat of the bench stone at about four in the afternoon at one hundred and sixty-eight pence out of that yard's own figures, twice, neither time thanked, and he said that the nineteenth and the twentieth days of August past are not in the bag and are not going in. A copyist of about fifty-nine, twenty-two years in a room off that market, who has never once asked what she is copying and gave the reason, being that a copyist who stops copying is a copyist who has admitted she copied something, and who sold him one sheet for a penny out of his own hand. A clerk of about sixty who has been in that room twenty-two years, is owed a quarter of a pound, has no book and no power, and said that he would not have thought that one was right. A man of about fifty with two papers on one table who told him the register copy of what this yard gave on the seventh of July is on a shelf behind that counter and has not been asked for in fifty-five days, and who has read a nine-line sheet four times and has not answered it and said the answer to a thing like that is a piece of paper with a name at the foot of it and not a word. A man of about thirty-one of the third lay with a chart in a bag who said that somebody would say the page was blank and not say why, and was told yes. A man of about thirty-eight with a boat of about thirteen tons and no papers on her who has been out on the sixth clause twice in six weeks on his own account and said so out loud on the second lay and asked for nothing. A man of about fifty-one on the crown of that mole with his page and his stone and no figure and **fifty days of silence and nothing given to him by anybody.**
8. **CHAPTER 410, THURSDAY THE SECOND OF SEPTEMBER. THE SECOND PAPER, AND THE FIGURE AT THE FOOT OF IT.** The refusal was taken down by the hand that wrote it and a second paper was pinned under the first at the same corner, carrying the same three lines naming two as permitted and one as present for the whole of the hour and the same three lines under them. **The hour is ten in the morning on the fifth day of October, being a Tuesday, at that door.** At the foot of it, where the first had a seal line, there are five lines in the clerk's own hand and no seal, and the reason the paper was held nine days is a figure, and the figure is seven: a copy of that thing, marked with where it came from, is seven hours at that bench and a pair of hands, and one hour is one, and both of those are true and neither of them cancels the other. **The holder read those five lines five times, did not knock, did not touch the door and went back down the hill. The room is entered once in these ten days and the second time in this volume is not this one's.**
9. **THE READ-BACK AT TEN PAST FIVE, ON THE FLAT OF THE BENCH STONE, WITH THE LIGHT NOT LIT.** The ship's hand read the leaf back in full in her own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, with both definitions of the four figures on the face of the reading, and stated that the fourth column has one hundred and twenty-five lines in it at the hour and one hundred and twenty-five at the close and has taken no line since the twenty-third of August, and that that is not a closure and not a strike-out.

### What is owed and what is not

**NOT OWED AND NOT TO BE RESTARTED BY ANY LATER PHASE: the whole of the standing inventory, which is entered in full on the last page and is not to be entered a second time in a hand-over; the hundred and twenty-fifth line, which is the last thing in that ledger and is not to be followed by a hundred and twenty-sixth in this volume or a later one; the forty-fourth wage Tuesday, which falls on Tuesday the twenty-fourth of August, outside this volume, and is not to be paid; a hundred and seventy-first day of the ninety; a sixteenth loss of flour; the custody room, which was not entered and is not to be entered until a later volume's own terms say so; the third of the three things and the claim on it, which is not withdrawn and which nobody is going to ask to have withdrawn; the new office, which is named once on one seal line and is in no mouth; the committed relationship, which begins once and is not a marriage and whose marriage is Volume 12's and is public; the new-volume question, which was asked once in a room with a clerk in it and is answered nowhere and is not to be answered by anybody who was in these fifty chapters; Alden Marr, who is not to be moved and whose partial confession is Volume 09's and whose original repair log is Volume 15's; and the plate at the fifth seam, in eleven feet, with its note open, not looked at, not measured, not touched, not asked about and not named, whose one advance in fifty chapters is a line of paper on a wall under glass in a city.**
